items.title: rplatypus rebuilt: deep learning for medical images in R
items.author: Michał Maj
items.description:

items.content:
[This article was first published on Data Science Guts, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

In October 2020 I wrote about platypus, an R package for object detection and image segmentation: YOLOv3 and U-Net in a few lines of R, on top of the keras and tensorflow packages. People used it. It collected 134 stars and a queue of issues – and then it quietly stopped working, and I stopped answering them.

This year I went back to it. Computer vision is the part of data science I enjoy most, and this package has always been my passion project – the place where I get to learn things my day job does not ask of me. What came out is not an update but a different package, with a new name, a different backend and a narrower purpose: rplatypus, deep learning for medical images in R. It has been submitted to CRAN and is waiting for review; until it is accepted, install it from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus")

This post is about why it had to be rewritten rather than fixed, what is in it now, and where the series of posts that follows is going.

Why the old one broke

R’s keras and tensorflow packages are not bindings to a C++ library. They are bridges, through reticulate, into a Python installation of TensorFlow – and in 2020 that was the Python installation, the one shared with everything else on the machine. Upgrade numpy for an unrelated project and an R session using platypus could stop loading. The failure never appeared in my package’s code, which made it miserable to support: the bug reports were about other people’s Python.

The second problem is the one that actually made me stop. platypus sat on two layers I did not control: the R keras and tensorflow packages on top of TensorFlow itself. When TensorFlow changed in Python, the R packages had to catch up before platypus could, and that often took a very long time. Until they did, my package was stuck, with issues I could not fix from my side. After enough of that, I lost the will to keep working on it.

Two things have changed since, and together they remove both problems at the root rather than patching around them.

reticulate learned to isolate. Since version 1.41, a package declares its Python requirements with py_require(), and reticulate builds a private environment for them with uv, cached and shared with nobody. There is no common Python left for two packages to fight over. rplatypus never touches a Python anyone else uses – and the person installing it never chooses an interpreter, activates anything or matches a version. The first call that needs the engine builds the environment; every call after that reuses it. And there is no R wrapper in between any more: rplatypus calls its own engine, which I release myself, so nothing waits for anybody else to catch up.

The medical imaging world settled on PyTorch. MONAI, nnU-Net, TorchIO, timm, the pretrained encoders and the foundation models – all of it is PyTorch. TensorFlow for medical images is effectively over, and the TensorFlow 2.9 the old engine was pinned to does not even install on Python 3.12. Staying would have meant rewriting anyway, onto a backend with no future in the field.

A third thing changed too. It does not fix the old failure, but it is the reason the rewrite happened at all instead of staying a good idea: writing a package got much cheaper. In 2020 I wrote every line of platypus myself, and the parts that make a package trustworthy – tests, documentation, error messages that say what went wrong – were the parts I never had time left for. This time I worked with an AI coding agent, Claude Code.

I want to be precise about what that means, because “AI wrote my package” is not it. The decisions were mine: what the package is for, which datasets to measure it on, what it should refuse, and what a result has to show before it goes into the documentation – every number in this series was measured, not generated. What the agent changed was the cost of everything around those decisions: writing the tests, keeping two packages in two languages in step, chasing a failing check through reticulate, uv and CUDA. That is exactly the work that used to end side projects like this one. The rewrite took around a month.

So the computation moved to pyplatypus, a Python engine on PyTorch, and rplatypus is the R package on top of it. The split is deliberate:

  • The engine is in Python, because that is where the models, the weights and the medical libraries already are. One codebase to maintain, and everything PyTorch has is within reach.
  • The product is in R, because that is where the gap is. Reading and combining masks, plotting, comparing models, the analysis around the network – that part is plain R and needs no Python at all.

I did consider native R torch, which binds libtorch directly and needs no Python. For one person maintaining this in their evenings it would have meant writing every architecture, loss and data pipeline twice, and giving up every pretrained weight in the Python ecosystem.

pyplatypus: the same engine, from Python

The engine is not hidden plumbing. pyplatypus is a package on PyPI in its own right – it too started life in 2022 on TensorFlow and was rewritten alongside – and if you work in Python you can use it directly:

pip install "pyplatypus[hub]"

The example below runs from both languages, out of one file.

The two are developed together, and in a fixed order. A feature lands in the engine first, the engine is published to PyPI, and only then does rplatypus move to it – each release of the R package pins one exact version of pyplatypus, so it cannot break because the engine changed underneath it. They also share one configuration format: the same YAML file describes the same experiment whichever language reads it, so an R user and a Python user can hand each other a run.

That is also how this series is written. The examples are in R, because that is where the gap is, and each post shows what the same step looks like from Python.

The gap

Here is the part that convinced me this was worth doing. R has excellent tools for reading medical images – RNifti, oro.dicom, divest – and a healthy deep learning stack. Almost nothing joins them. When I checked in September, the CRAN Task View for Medical Image Analysis (last updated August 2025) listed no deep learning packages at all.

So rplatypus is meant to be that missing piece: not a wrapper around a Python library you then have to learn, but an R package that happens to compute in Python.

A mask, without training anything

The quickest way to see whether a package does anything useful is to borrow a model someone already trained. rplatypus publishes weights by name – here a U-Net trained on the 2018 Data Science Bowl, the same nuclei dataset I used on this blog in 2020.

The folder nuclei/ holds four microscopy images in the dataset’s own layout – one directory per image, with images/ and masks/ inside.

library(rplatypus)

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("nuclei", "nuclei", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("nuclei", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
fit <- platypus_fit(spec, verbose = FALSE)
masks <- predict(fit, split = "validation")
dim(masks)
#> [1]   4 256 256

Four images, 256 by 256 pixels, one class label per pixel. This ran on the processor, with no GPU; platypus_device() tells you whether yours will use one, and why not if it can’t.

images <- list.files("nuclei", pattern = "[.]png$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
images <- read_images(grep("/images/", images, value = TRUE), size = c(256, 256))
plot_masks(images, prediction = masks, colormap = binary_colormap)

The first three are fluorescence images, and the nuclei come out as clean blobs. The fourth is a brightfield image of stained cells, and the model finds specks - the small dark nuclei inside the cells. That is the hard kind of image in this dataset, and the next post looks at it closely.

There is no score here, and that is on purpose. These four images come from the same collection the weights were trained on, so any number measured on them would flatter the model. The numbers that mean something were measured on a held-out split when the weights were published, and available_weights() says what they are and what the model cannot do - for instance, that it is a semantic model, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong.

The same thing from a file

The same specification can live in a file. This one started as save_spec(spec, "nuclei.yaml"), with the lists tidied by hand:

nuclei.yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: nuclei
  validation_path: nuclei
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
- name: nuclei
  architecture: u_net
  input_shape: [256, 256]
  blocks: 4
  filters: 16
  weights: dsbowl-unet
  fit: false

Reading it back gives exactly the object built from arguments above:

identical(as.list(platypus_spec("nuclei.yaml")), as.list(spec))
#> [1] TRUE

So platypus_fit(platypus_spec("nuclei.yaml")) does everything the R code did, and nothing downstream can tell which way the specification was written. The Python engine reads the very same file:

from pyplatypus import build_engine, from_yaml

engine = build_engine(from_yaml("nuclei.yaml"))
engine.fit()  # with `fit: false` this loads the published weights instead of training
masks = engine.predict("nuclei", split="validation")

A configuration file and an R script describe the same experiment, and either can be handed to a colleague - whichever language they work in.

What is in it

Briefly, because most of these get their own post:

  • Segmentation, 2D and 3D: U-Net, U-Net++, Res-U-Net and LinkNet, eleven losses, five metrics that can leave the background out - which matters when the background is most of the image.
  • Classification - one label for a whole image, scored by AUC rather than accuracy, because a classifier that answers “no finding” where 3% have one scores 0.97 and has learnt nothing.
  • Object detection with YOLOv3, with anchors fitted to your boxes rather than borrowed from COCO.
  • Instance segmentation - a count of objects instead of an area.
  • Volumes: NIfTI and DICOM in, with voxel spacing handled, a split by patient rather than by slice, and results in millilitres rather than voxels.
  • A score per case, not one per dataset, so the worst image has a name.
  • Refusals before a wasted day: a colormap that matches none of your masks, channels in an order you did not intend, a DICOM series with a missing slice - each stopped before training, by name.
  • One specification - from R arguments or from a YAML file, read the same way by the Python engine.

The full reference and seven vignettes, six of them precomputed from real runs, are at maju116.github.io/rplatypus.

This is where the package starts, not where it ends. The U-Net family, YOLOv3 and the classifier are the first models in it, not the only ones that will be: more architectures are coming, along with what is still missing - multi-label classification, ensembling, boxes in three dimensions. Which of those comes first depends partly on what people actually need, which is one more reason for the question at the end of this post.

Development is moving fast right now, and CRAN asks for new versions no more often than every month or two, so once the package is on CRAN, install.packages("rplatypus") will usually be a step behind. The GitHub version above will always be the newest.

What comes next

This is the first post of a series. Each of the next ones takes one dataset and one thing that measurement on it taught me:

  1. Nuclei, five years later - a model with a mean Dice of 0.855 that scores 0.006 on three images, and why the mean could not tell you.
  2. Classification - a classifier with 0.97 accuracy that has learnt nothing, and why balanced accuracy does not rescue it.
  3. Blood cells and YOLOv3 - anchors, and why a point of mAP across five seeds is noise.
  4. CT volumes - a Dice of 0.88 and volumes 12-23% too large, which is not a contradiction.
  5. Retinal vessels - why you cannot resize a vessel nine pixels wide.
  6. Counting touching nuclei - 245 objects or 180, from the same forward pass.
  7. Pretrained encoders - measured on three modalities, where a 1.9M-parameter encoder beats ResNet-34 on two of them.

One question for you

Everything above rests on an assumption I have not been able to test: that people do medical image analysis in R and would rather stay in R to do deep learning on it. If that is you - or if it is your lab, and you went to Python because there was nothing here - I would really like to hear about it. Open an issue, write to me at michalmaj116@gmail.com, or find me on LinkedIn.

And one more thing, since this is a good place to say it: I am looking for my next role. If your team works on computer vision, medical imaging, or any problem where a model has to be measured honestly before anyone trusts it, I would be glad to talk - the same email works.

items.title: Agents in Production: Build Your First AI Agent in R with {ellmer}
items.author: The Jumping Rivers Blog
items.content:
[This article was first published on The Jumping Rivers Blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

This is part one of a five-part series on putting AI agents into production with R. Each part builds on the same app, a clinical trial safety assistant. The parts are:

  • From Chatbot to Agent (this post)
  • Putting the Agent in a Shiny App
  • Can You Trust It?
  • Audit Trails, Costs and Models
  • Sharing Your Tools with MCP

We asked Gemini how many people on the high dose of a drug had itching in a well-known clinical trial. It said 21, and sounded sure of it. We asked again and got 25, with different numbers for the other groups too. Both answers cited the trial’s data files, but the model hadn’t been given them. It was answering from memory, so neither answer could be checked.

In this series we build an assistant whose numbers you can check. The model picks an R function, and R does the counting. We tell the model never to do the maths itself, and part 3 checks that it doesn’t. It can still ask R the wrong question, so every result says what was counted.

No pharma background is needed, since the pattern works for any data your team asks about. Later parts add a Shiny app, tests, limits on who sees patient records, an audit trail, and a way to share the tools with other AI agents.

What is an AI agent?

A chatbot answers from what it learned in training. An AI agent can also ask your code to do things, which is called tool calling (or function calling).

You give the model a list of tools, each with a name, a description and its arguments. When a question needs a tool, the model replies with a request instead of an answer, such as “run count_subjects() with arm = "Placebo"”.

Your code runs the function and sends back the result. This repeats until the model has enough to answer, and that cycle is the agent loop.

The model never runs your code. It can only ask. Your R session decides what runs and what goes back.

{ellmer} runs this loop for you. You write ordinary R functions, describe them and register them with a chat. New to {ellmer}? Our LLMs in R & Python webinar is a good start. As the {ellmer} tool-calling guide recommends, all exact computation happens inside the tools.

What you need

Get this part’s folder from our blog repository, by cloning the repository or downloading it as a ZIP file, and open it as a project in R 4.5. The project uses {renv} to pin every package version, so run this once:

install.packages("renv")
renv::restore()

If you’d rather not use {renv}, install the packages yourself, though you’ll get newer versions than we tested:

install.packages(c("ellmer", "pharmaverseadam", "dplyr", "jsonlite"))

You’ll also need a Gemini API key, and our alt-text post shows how to get one. To store it, run file.edit(".Renviron") in the project, add the line GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key, save the file and restart R. The code’s README has more setup tips, for Windows in particular.

The free tier is fine here, because this trial’s data is public, but not for your own patient or confidential data. Google’s terms also require the paid service for any app offered to users in the UK, the EEA or Switzerland (more on this in part 4).

We tested everything with R 4.5.1, {ellmer} 0.5.0 and {pharmaverseadam} 1.3.0 in September 2026. {ellmer} changes quickly, so if something behaves differently, check your versions first.

The trial data

Our example is CDISC pilot study 01, a worked example published by CDISC, the body that sets clinical trial data standards. It tested a skin patch of an experimental drug, xanomeline, in people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s disease. Participants, called subjects in trial data, wore a placebo, low-dose or high-dose patch for 26 weeks.

The {pharmaverseadam} package rebuilds the study’s analysis datasets in CDISC’s ADaM format, and we need two of them: adsl, with one row per subject, and adae, with one row per adverse event. An adverse event is anything medically unwanted that happened to a subject during the trial, whether or not the drug caused it.

Trial terms, in plain English

  • Arm: a treatment group, here placebo, low dose (54 mg) or high dose (81 mg, after two weeks at 54 mg).
  • Screen failure: someone assessed who didn’t join the trial.
  • Safety population: everyone who had at least one dose. Safety results count this group.
  • Treatment-emergent: an adverse event that started, or got worse, after the first dose and no later than a set window after the last one (14 days, in this data).
  • Serious adverse event: one with a serious outcome, such as death, a threat to life, a hospital stay or lasting disability. Intensity is recorded separately, as severity (mild, moderate or severe), so a severe headache need not be serious. In the data, the AESER flag marks serious events, and our tools count that flag.
  • Preferred term and body system (or system organ class): each event is coded with a standard medical dictionary, MedDRA. “Itchy skin” becomes the preferred term PRURITUS, in the body system “skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders”.
  • Application site: where the patch was worn. Erythema means redness.

Our tools count the way a safety table usually does, and two of their choices are easy to miss. Both change every count:

  • Not everyone in adsl joined the trial. Of its 306 people, 52 are screen failures, so the safety population (SAFFL == "Y") is 254 subjects.
  • Planned and received treatment can differ. Each subject has a planned arm (ARM) and the treatment they received (ACTARM). Twelve subjects randomised to the high dose stopped within two weeks, before their dose went up to 81 mg, so here they count as low dose.

If you work with trial data, the note for pharma readers near the end covers a few choices a formal analysis plan might make differently.

The tools also keep only the treatment-emergent events (TRTEMFL == "Y"), which leaves 1,122 of the 1,191 event rows. One function, in R/data.R, does all of this:

ARMS <- c("Placebo", "Xanomeline Low Dose", "Xanomeline High Dose")

load_trial_data <- function() {
 subjects <- pharmaverseadam::adsl |>
 dplyr::filter(SAFFL == "Y") |>
 dplyr::select(USUBJID, ACTARM, AGE, SEX, RACE)
 events <- pharmaverseadam::adae |>
 dplyr::filter(TRTEMFL %in% "Y", USUBJID %in% subjects$USUBJID) |>
 dplyr::select(USUBJID, ACTARM, AEDECOD, AETERM, AEBODSYS, AESER, AESEV, ASTDT)
 list(
 subjects = subjects,
 events = events,
 # Every term and body system recorded in the trial, including the few
 # never treatment-emergent, so asking about them gives a real zero.
 terms = sort(unique(pharmaverseadam::adae$AEDECOD)),
 body_systems = sort(unique(pharmaverseadam::adae$AEBODSYS))
 )
}

Join us for our AI in Production conference! For more details, check out our conference website!

Asking without tools

We started by asking gemini-3.7-flash the opening question twice, with no tools:

# Without tools, the model can only guess.
bare <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini()
bare$chat("In CDISC pilot study 01, how many subjects on high-dose xanomeline had pruritus?", echo = "output")

Pruritus is itching. Both answers are pasted as they came back, Markdown and all, except that their headings are shown in bold.

Pedro
In CDISC pilot study 01, how many subjects on high-dose xanomeline had pruritus?
Gemini, first try

In the CDISC Pilot Study 01 (Safety Pilot), 21 subjects (or 25.0%) in the Xanomeline High-Dose group had the adverse event pruritus.

Summary Breakdown for Pruritus (Treatment-Emergent AEs):

  • Placebo ($N = 86$): 2 subjects (2.3%)
  • Xanomeline Low Dose (54 mg) ($N = 84$): 11 subjects (13.1%)
  • Xanomeline High Dose (81 mg) ($N = 84$): 21 subjects (25.0%)

(Source: CDISC Pilot 01 Table 14-4.01 / ADAE dataset, Preferred Term: Pruritus under the System Organ Class “Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders”)

Gemini, second try

In the CDISC Pilot Study 01 (evaluating Xanomeline vs. Placebo in Alzheimer’s Disease), 25 subjects in the Xanomeline High Dose treatment group experienced Pruritus (MedDRA Preferred Term: PRURITUS).

Context & Breakdown across Treatment Arms:

  • Placebo ($N = 86$): 5 subjects (5.8%)
  • Xanomeline Low Dose ($N = 84$): 18 subjects (21.4%)
  • Xanomeline High Dose ($N = 84$): 25 subjects (29.8%)

(Source: CDISC SDTM/ADaM Pilot Project 01 Adverse Events Analysis Dataset, ADAE)

Neither answer matches the data we hold, but each high-dose figure is a correct number for something else:

High-dose pruritus Where the number comes from
First answer 21 of 84 (25.0%) The low dose’s count, over the planned arm size
Second answer 25 of 84 (29.8%) The right count, over the planned arm size
The data 25 of 72 (34.7%) Treatment-emergent, by treatment received

On placebo, the data says 8 of 86 (9.3%), and the other counts in both answers match nothing.

The second answer is the more dangerous one. Its count is right, and only the arm size differs from ours, so it survives a quick check. And nothing in either answer says which data, which population or which events it counted.

Writing the tools

The model never sees a tool’s code, only its description, so the description is what tells it when to use the tool. Most of the work happens in count_subjects(), in R/tools.R:

count_subjects <- function(data, arm = NULL, serious_only = FALSE, term = NULL, body_system = NULL) {
 arm <- check_arm(arm)
 serious_only <- check_flag(serious_only, "serious_only")
 term <- check_known(
 check_string(term, "term"), data$terms, "preferred term",
 "Call ae_summary to see the terms used in this trial."
 )
 body_system <- check_known(
 check_string(body_system, "body_system"), data$body_systems, "body system",
 "Call ae_summary with by = 'body_system' to see them."
 )
 data <- filter_arm(data, arm)
 events <- data$events
 if (serious_only) events <- dplyr::filter(events, AESER == "Y")
 if (!is.null(term)) events <- dplyr::filter(events, AEDECOD == term)
 if (!is.null(body_system)) events <- dplyr::filter(events, AEBODSYS == body_system)
 n <- dplyr::n_distinct(events$USUBJID)
 total <- nrow(data$subjects)
 jsonlite::toJSON(list(
 arm = arm %||% "All arms",
 # Say what was counted, so a wrong reading of the question shows.
 filters = list(
 serious_only = serious_only,
 term = term %||% "any",
 body_system = body_system %||% "any"
 ),
 subjects_with_event = n,
 subjects_in_arm = total,
 percent = round(100 * n / total, 1)
 ), auto_unbox = TRUE)
}

Four choices matter most:

  • It returns JSON. The model reads text, and {ellmer} 0.5.0 deprecates returning data frames from tools.
  • It says what it counted. The result repeats the filters it applied, so if the model misread the question, you can see it.
  • Unknown input is an error, never a zero. Ask for a term the trial doesn’t have and the tool fails, with a message telling the model how to recover. A zero that means “I didn’t understand” is worse than no answer.
  • Every argument is checked. Models don’t always send the types they’re asked for, and in part 5 other programs call these tools over MCP, a standard way for AI apps to share tools.

We added that last check after a problem in testing. Passing serious_only = "true", as text rather than TRUE, made the tool quietly count every subject with any adverse event. It answered 217 instead of 3.

Because it’s an ordinary R function, you can call it without a model. Source the files in R/ first:

for (file in list.files("R", pattern = "[.]R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(file)
count_subjects(load_trial_data(), arm = "Xanomeline High Dose", term = "PRURITUS")
#> {"arm":"Xanomeline High Dose","filters":{"serious_only":false,"term":"PRURITUS","body_system":"any"},"subjects_with_event":25,"subjects_in_arm":72,"percent":34.7}

The tool definition is what the model sees:

ellmer::tool(
 function(arm = NULL, serious_only = FALSE, term = NULL, body_system = NULL) {
 count_subjects(data, arm, serious_only, term, body_system)
 },
 name = "count_subjects",
 description = paste(
 "Count subjects in the safety population with at least one treatment-emergent",
 "adverse event matching the filters. Returns the count, the number of subjects",
 "in the arm and the percentage."
 ),
 arguments = list(
 arm = arm_type,
 serious_only = ellmer::type_boolean("Only count serious adverse events.", required = FALSE),
 term = ellmer::type_string(
 "MedDRA preferred term, e.g. 'PRURITUS'. Leave out to count any event.",
 required = FALSE
 ),
 body_system = ellmer::type_string(
 "MedDRA body system, e.g. 'NERVOUS SYSTEM DISORDERS'. Leave out for any.",
 required = FALSE
 )
 ),
 annotations = ellmer::tool_annotations(title = "Counting subjects", read_only_hint = TRUE)
)

The annotations give the tool a title, which part 2’s app uses to label each tool call. The arm is an enum, a fixed list of allowed values, so the model sees the three valid arms:

arm_type <- ellmer::type_enum(ARMS, "Treatment arm. Leave out to cover all arms.", required = FALSE)

check_arm() still rejects anything else, for callers that ignore the list. In all, trial_tools() builds four tools around one copy of the data: list_arms() for arm sizes, ae_summary() for the most common events, count_subjects(), and subject_profile() for one patient’s record.

Running the loop

One small function in R/agent.R puts the agent together, creating a Gemini chat with the system prompt (next section) and registering the tools:

make_agent <- function(tools = trial_tools(), prompt_path = "prompts/system.md",
 model = NULL, chat_fun = ellmer::chat_google_gemini) {
 chat <- chat_fun(system_prompt = read_prompt(prompt_path), model = model)
 chat$register_tools(tools)
 chat
}

With model = NULL you get {ellmer} 0.5.0’s default, gemini-3.7-flash. That default changes between releases, so part 4 pins the model by name.

Switching provider is usually one argument, such as make_agent(chat_fun = ellmer::chat_anthropic), though local models through chat_ollama() have a catch that part 4 covers.

We asked two questions with echo = "all", which prints the question, every tool request and every result, as well as the answer. Below are the tool requests and some of the results. We’ve kept the high dose’s ae_summary() result in full, so you can match it to the answer.

chat <- make_agent()
chat$chat("Which adverse events were most common on the high dose, compared with placebo?", echo = "all")
chat$chat("How many subjects had a serious adverse event, and on which arms?", echo = "all")
Pedro
Which adverse events were most common on the high dose, compared with placebo?
< [tool request (ae_summary)]: ae_summary(arm = "Xanomeline High Dose", by =
< "term", top_n = 10L)
< [tool request (ae_summary)]: ae_summary(arm = "Placebo", by = "term", top_n =
< 10L)

Across all arms, 3 subjects (1.2%) out of 254 had a serious adverse event:

  • Placebo: 0 subjects (0.0%) of 86
  • Xanomeline Low Dose: 2 subjects (2.1%) of 96
  • Xanomeline High Dose: 1 subject (1.4%) of 72

We never told the model which tools to use. For the first question, it called ae_summary() once per arm for the top ten events. Four of the high dose’s ten weren’t in placebo’s, so it counted those on placebo with count_subjects() before it answered. For the second, it called count_subjects() with serious_only = TRUE for all arms together, then for each arm. Every number in both answers appears in a tool result.

To run all of this yourself, source("demo/part-1.R") asks the no-tools question and both agent questions, which takes about six requests. The offline tests run with source("tests/run.R") and make no API calls.

The system prompt

The system prompt sets the rules for every conversation:

You answer questions about the safety data of one clinical trial: CDISC pilot study 01, which compared a xanomeline skin patch at two doses with placebo.

- Use the tools for every fact about the trial. Every number in your answer must appear in a tool result from this conversation. Never calculate, estimate or remember numbers yourself.
- Quote numbers exactly as the tools give them.
- Say which arm each number is for. Counts are subjects in the safety population, by the treatment they actually received, with treatment-emergent adverse events.
- If the tools cannot answer a question, say so.
- Keep answers short.

Two lines do most of the work. The first, that every number must come from a tool, is the rule the rest of the series tests. The third makes the model name the arm and population, so a reader always has a denominator to check.

A prompt is still only a request, and a model can ignore it. That’s why part 3 adds a check on where each number came from.

Why narrow tools

You could give the model a single run_r_code() tool and let it answer anything. But then you’d be validating whatever code it happened to write that day.

A narrow tool can be tested against numbers checked by hand, logged, and allowed or refused on its own. It’s easier for the model too, since picking the right tool is a smaller job than writing correct {dplyr} code.

What could still go wrong

The agent works, but it isn’t ready for a team yet:

  • The model invents or rounds a number anyway. The prompt only asks it not to. Part 3 checks every answer’s numbers against the tool results.
  • Patient-level data. Right now the model can open any patient’s record. Part 3 limits subject_profile() to a reviewer group, whose members confirm each record before it opens, and part 5 leaves it out of the tools shared with other AI agents.
  • Many users at once. A console session suits one person. In part 2’s Shiny app, each person gets their own conversation.
  • Cost and outages. Within minutes, the free tier sent us “503 high demand” and “429 quota exceeded” errors. It’s small, too: when we wrote this, about 20 requests a day per model, and a question takes one request per round of tool calls. {ellmer} tries each request up to three times by default, and options(ellmer_max_tries = …) changes that. Parts 2 and 4 deal with the rest.

A note for pharma readers

Our counts follow {pharmaverseadam}, which rebuilds the pilot’s analysis datasets from its SDTM data. A formal analysis plan might settle three of its choices differently:

  • Treatment received. {pharmaverseadam} takes the arm each subject received from the SDTM data, which moves the twelve early stoppers to the low dose, and its TRT01A matches ACTARM. The pilot’s own analysis datasets kept them on the high dose (TRT01A equals TRT01P, giving 86, 84 and 84), so the second no-tools answer’s 25 of 84 may well be the original study’s figure.
  • Serious events. Like the pilot’s own analysis, our tools count the AESER flag, which is set on only three treatment-emergent events. Another 33 meet a seriousness criterion with AESER = "N", including three deaths, two of them on placebo. A study team would query that with data management.
  • Rounding. R’s round() sends an exact half to the even digit, so 6 of 96 low-dose subjects with skin irritation (6.25%) shows as 6.2%, where SAS would print 6.3%. That happens once in this data.

In Python

In chatlas (pip install "chatlas[google]"), a function’s type hints and docstring define the tool, and a Literal type makes the arm an enum:

from typing import Literal

from chatlas import ChatGoogle

def count_subjects(
 arm: Literal["Placebo", "Xanomeline Low Dose", "Xanomeline High Dose"] | None = None,
 serious_only: bool = False,
 term: str | None = None,
) -> str:
 """Count subjects in the safety population with at least one
 treatment-emergent adverse event matching the filters."""
 ... # the same counting, with polars or pandas

chat = ChatGoogle(model="gemini-3.7-flash", system_prompt=open("prompts/system.md").read())
chat.register_tool(count_subjects)
chat.chat("Which adverse events were most common on the high dose?")

Summary

An agent is a model, some tools and a loop. The model decides what to count, R does the counting on carefully filtered data, and the prompt asks the model to quote only what the tools return.

Without tools, it gave us two confident answers that disagreed, and neither matched our data. With tools, every number came from R.

Next time, we put the agent in a Shiny app, so that several people can use it at once.

All the code for this part, including demo/part-1.R and the tests, is in our blog repository.
